new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (6 pp..bb70; PDF title "Microsoft Word - Angor_agg (Unicode Compliant)"). extracted text gives, on page 4 under the heading "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)": "Stress is phonemic. Examples: a'ri 'tree sp.' 'arɨ 'string bag' / a'mboko 'beetle' ama'ro 'she sits' / mana'ŋgo 'she stands' ma'naŋgo 'mushroom sp.'" -- identical to the reported quote apart from column whitespace. The surrounding section gives no placement rule and no secondary stress; the only other stress-related line on p. 4 is the elision remark ("Final unstressed vowel, especially /ə/, tends to be elided.."), as the report says. Identity: the OPD header reads "Angor (Anggor, Senagi, Watapor, Bibriari) Language [AG…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Angor: the same segmental string can carry stress on different syllables with a change of meaning (a'ri vs 'arɨ; a'mboko vs ama'ro; mana'ŋgo vs ma'naŋgo). The source gives no default placement rule, so stress must be treated as lexically specified; the minimal pairs show stress on the first, second or third syllable of two- and three-syllable words. No tone or length contrast is mentioned under the suprasegmentals heading.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Related remark p.4 (Conventions: Phonological): 'Final unstressed vowel, especially /ə/, tends to be elided in speech after voiceless plosives /p t k/, prenasalized plosives /ᵐb ⁿd/ and /m n ŋ x/.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; the six-page OPD cites isolated citation-form words only (no phrase-level or sentence-stress discussion). The statement is a one-line survey-format entry in an unreviewed SIL draft, not a full phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers Angor [agg] = ango1254 as spoken around Biwan and Koareamon villages, Amanab district, Sandaun Province (alternate names Anggor, Senagi, Watapor, Bibriari); no dialect split is named, so the statement applies to the language as a whole. Note for the earlier scan record: 'Litteral & Litteral 1974, Anggor' is an anthropology text in McElhanon (ed.) Legends from Papua New Guinea, not a phonology write-up; the phonology item is the 1997 OPD.

new_statements.quote: It is the domain within which stress rules operate. Stress is contrastive in Angor as in the following examples: mánanggo (má.na.ŋgo) ‘it was, it stood’ manánggo (ma.ná.ŋgo) ‘species of mushroom’ [...] The nucleus of the foot, or primary stress, may occur on the ultima, asifú ‘he is going up’, the penult manánggo ‘species of mushroom’ or the antepenult sánggiri ‘bird of paradise’. Syllables following the nucleus are unstressed. Every alternate syllable preceding the nucleus has secondary stress except when the syllable has the vowels i or ü in its nucleus, in which case the secondary stress occurs on the preceding syllable.

Syllables following the nucleus are unstressed. Every alternate syllable preceding the nucleus has secondary stress exc…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's existing statement (Litteral 1997 OPD, 'Stress is phonemic', minimal pairs incl. mana'ŋgo / ma'naŋgo) and adds the domain (foot = phonological word), the three possible primary positions (ultima, penult, antepenult), the alternating secondary-stress rule with the i/ü shift, the ban on stressed foot-final i, and stress shift under -mbo suffixation. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; this source supports filling it as lexical (unpredictable primary stress within the last three syllables).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) at the level of the foot = phonological word. Primary stress is lexically placed and may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (minimal pair mánanggo 'it was, it stood' vs manánggo 'mushroom sp.'). Syllables after the primary are unstressed. Three phonetic degrees of stress, but only the primary need be marked because the rest is predictable from the primary by rule ('The stress rules for the foot operate from the end of the foot forward', p. 24). Phonemic stress is written with an acute on the nuclear vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 24: 'Every alternate syllable preceding the nucleus has secondary stress except when the syllable has the vowels i or ü in its nucleus, in which case the secondary stress occurs on the preceding syllable.' Example: asifú (secondary on a, the second syllable before the primary; the syllable directly before the primary is unstressed); hoemariheyándi (hwemàriheyándi) 'I saw it' — secondary moved one syllable left because the expected syllable has i.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 24: 'Foot final i is never stressed' (and may be elided utterance-finally after fricatives or stops, e.g. ro aháhi (ro agáx)). Intonation: the nonfinal falling contour has a rapidly falling F0 'on the final stressed syllable of the contour' (p. 24). Chapter V: progressive vowel harmony 'when an unstressed mid central vowel becomes stressed with the affixation of -mbo' (gad-efi > gad-efo-mbo), i.e. suffixation can move stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources are Robert Litteral's own descriptions of Angor (Anggor) of Amanab, Sandaun (West Sepik) Province; no dialect is singled out. The 2008 file is the reformatted version of the 1980 UPenn dissertation (SIL PNG 'Dissertation # 9664'), so works 0, 1 and 2 are three catalogue entries for one underlying text.

sources.note: Now downloaded: this is both of the first reader's high-priority works still to obtain (the 1980 UPenn dissertation and its 2008 SIL reformatting are the same work). It gives the full stress statement -- contrastive primary stress on ultima, penult or antepenult; syllables after the nucleus unstressed; alternating secondary stress before the nucleus with an i/ü exception; foot-final i never stressed -- and should replace the 6-page OPD as the statement of record.
